abstract: Contributing to the design of functional graphene nanoribbons (GNRs) structures, we have synthesized porous and doped armchair graphene nanoribbons (N-GNRs) on Cu(111), Ag(100), and Ag(110) with atomic precision. The structural characterization and reaction step have been investigated using scanning tunneling microscopy. Despite pronounced differences in surface symmetry and chemical reactivity, the hierarchical polymerization of 2,7,11,16-tetrabromotetrabenzo[a,c,h,j]phenazine (TBTBP) through the on-surface Ullmann coupling consistently yields porous nitrogen-doped graphene nanoribbons with identical backbone structure, periodic pore architecture, and site-specific nitrogen doping. While ribbon length and growth kinetics vary across substrates—being limited on Cu(111), intermediate on Ag(100), and extended on Ag(110)—the intermolecular spacing and armchair edge topology remain preserved. These results demonstrate that the intrinsic molecular design of TBTBP dominates over substrate symmetry in defining the final nanoribbon structure. The substrate tolerance and structural fidelity observed here highlight the potential of this precursor platform for the synthesis of atomically precise porous GNRs on diverse supports, providing a promising route toward their integration on technologically relevant substrates.

title: Bayesian model selection for graphite oxidation by molecular oxygen informed by new data
abstract: Flow tube experiments and Bayesian model selection and calibration methods are used to assess kinetics models for graphite oxidation at pressures of 33 and 330 Pa and temperatures from 1100 to 2284 K. Bayesian methods, which are well established but not commonly used for carbon oxidation modeling, are employed to select and calibrate models based on the novel experiments. The experiments isolate high-temperature gas-surface interactions and mass loss, enabling low-computational-cost model evaluations, extensive statistical sampling, and inference methods, which evaluate oxidation rate models even though oxidation rates themselves are not directly measured. Influential reaction parameters are selected by global sensitivity analysis and parameter influence criteria. Bayesian inference is used for both parameter calibration and model class selection among three candidate model classes proposed for air–carbon ablation. The two classes with dual adsorption mechanisms, in which oxygen can adsorb strongly or weakly, are shown to be more plausible than the model with a single adsorption mechanism, though both are supported equally. All models predict that CO production increases with temperature until a peak is reached. Models with dual adsorption mechanisms differ by their prediction of CO and CO 2 product ratios. Posterior distributions of calibration parameters are constructed to quantify parameter uncertainties and model errors for uncertainty quantification when using these models.

abstract: Biomass-derived graphene quantum dots (GQDs) exhibit favorable photoluminescence characteristics; however, mechanistic interpretation and reproducible emission tuning remain challenging because conventional tuning routes often co-vary dot geometry, surface chemistry, and internal ordering. Here, we develop an oxidant-free supercritical carbon dioxide (ScCO 2 ) conversion strategy that constrains GQD geometry while enabling upstream structural programming of the carbon framework. Bamboo biochar was pyrolyzed at 750–1150 °C to tune in-plane sp 2 coherence and then converted into GQDs under identical ScCO 2 conditions. Across the series, the as-prepared GQDs remain ultrasmall few-layer platelets within a narrow geometry window, whereas their in-plane lattice ordering depends strongly on the precursor pyrolysis temperature, as reflected by an increased fraction of sixfold-symmetric FFT features. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and thermogravimetric analysis indicate that oxygen-related metrics and residual ash content vary across the series but do not show a trend-consistent correspondence with the optical evolution. Optical characterization reveals a persistent dominant emission band near 440 nm for all samples, while the highest-temperature product, 1150GQD, develops a distinct long-wavelength shoulder around 475 nm together with enhanced excitation selectivity in photoluminescence excitation spectra. These results establish a separable design in which precursor microstructure biases in-plane lattice ordering in ScCO 2 -derived GQDs under a geometry-constrained conversion window, providing a more interpretable basis for ordering-correlated photoluminescence modulation in biomass-derived luminescent nanocarbons.

abstract: Metal-catalyzed graphitization plays a critical role in the conversion of biochar into sustainable carbon materials. However, the catalytic mechanisms governing the synthesis of graphene-layered structures remain poorly understood. Herein, we investigate the catalytic effect of Fe–Ca bimetallic systems on the graphitization of cellulose-derived biochar (biocarbon) by combining high-energy synchrotron X-ray total scattering with Pair Distribution Function (PDF) analysis. The results show that bimetallic catalysis promotes the transformation of amorphous and turbostratic carbon into medium- and long-range ordered graphitic carbon arrangements, presenting enhanced crystallinity compared to monometallic catalysts. The graphitization mechanism is explained by combination of thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and high-resolution X-ray total scattering analysis. Further Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations identify a stable Fe(110)–graphene interface with strong chemisorption, characterized by high binding energy and short interfacial distance, which facilitates charge transfer and orbital hybridization at the metal–carbon interface. These findings represent a step forward in understanding the catalytic process of enhanced graphitization in bimetallic systems and provide original insights into the role of metal–carbon interactions in catalytic carbon restructuring processes. We believe that these findings make an important contribution to understanding and predicting the thermophysical, thermoelectrical and thermochemical properties of carbonaceous materials derived from renewable resources for energy storage and environmental applications.

abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), such as perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), pose significant risks to health and the environment due to their chemical resistance. Here, we compare the photocatalytic performance of standalone carbon photocatalysts based on diamond nanomaterials. We demonstrate the complete mineralization of PFOA under solar-type illumination using highly crystalline hydrogenated milled nanodiamonds (H-MND). Mechanism investigations reveal two distinct degradation pathways: chain-shortening and defluorination reaction through F/OH substitution which appears specific to H-MND and absent in other types of nanodiamonds. This selectivity is attributed to the unique negative electron affinity of H-MND and their enhanced surface hydrophobicity. Notably, PFOA photodegradation in presence of H-MND arises efficiently under 300–400 nm illumination, deep UV (250-300 nm) only accelerating the process. Under comparable conditions, H-MND outperforms conventional standalone photocatalysts, even in aerobic environments and under solar-type irradiation. These findings highlight the potential of H-MND to serve as an effective solution for PFAS remediation, whether used as a simple and reusable standalone photocatalyst or integrated into more advanced hybrid systems.

title: Deciphering proximal effects in substituted carbon nanozymes: Modulating ROS recognition and enhancing catalytic activity
abstract: Proximal effects between functional groups in substituted carbon nanozymes can influence their activity towards reactive oxygen species (ROS). However, their molecular-level understanding remains limited, restricting full utilization. Herein, we combine molecular dynamics and quantum mechanics calculations to reveal how proximal functional group effects regulate ROS recognition and catalytic activity. The results demonstrate that each isolated functional group can provide a limited thermodynamically favorable region for ROS recognition, within which the binding strength can overcome the diffusion trends of ROS. The strongest ROS binding occurs when the -COO - group binds to H 2 O 2 ; however, H 2 O 2 enrichment is limited to within ∼12 Å, beyond which H 2 O 2 tends to diffuse away. Other ROS exhibit even weaker binding affinities and smaller recognition ranges, from 4 to 8 Å. Thus, proximity groups may regulate ROS recognition through steric hindrance, competitive binding, and cooperativity, while also inducing intramolecular hydrogen bonding that can either hinder or enhance ROS binding. QM calculations focus on the activity of -OH substituted nanozymes toward H 2 O 2 . Positioning -OH groups on rings with a single exposed C–H site results in higher activity than placement on rings with three exposed C–H sites, while appropriate positioning of additional proximal -OH groups further promotes H 2 O 2 activation, lowering the activation energy by 3.2 and 2.4 kcal/mol, respectively. These results indicate that designing nanozymes with synergistic proximal effects between functional groups is promising for enhancing their activity.

abstract: Multispectral compatible stealth materials are essential for modern military platforms to counter diverse detection threats. However, the inherent mechanism conflict between microwave absorption and infrared stealth hampers cross-band stealth in single-material systems. Herein, 2D Cu-HHTP/rGO functional fillers are embedded into a solid-solid phase change polyurethane (SHPEG) matrix to fabricate a flexible, self-healing composite film (Cu-HHTP/rGO/SHPEG) with radar-infrared dual-stealth. A synergistic regulation strategy of Schottky heterointerfaces and electrical conductivity is proposed, which induces a built-in electric field and optimizes dielectric loss. Cu-HHTP/rGO attains outstanding microwave absorption with a minimum reflection loss (RLmin) of -60.49 dB and an effective absorption bandwidth (EAB) of 7.51 GHz. Meanwhile, the dynamic cross-linking network modified with disulfide bonds ensures self-healing ability and structural stability of the SHPEG matrix. Based on the excellent thermal management capacity of SHPEG and the low infrared emissivity of Cu-HHTP/rGO, the Cu-HHTP/rGO/SHPEG film possesses remarkable integrated performance: RLmin reaching -52.8 dB, EAB covering 7.29 GHz, infrared emissivity as low as 0.240 and a phase transition enthalpy of 95.1 J/g. The composite film also exhibits exceptional flexibility, self-healing efficiency, shape stability and mechanical strength. This work provides new insights for resolving multiband stealth conflicts and promotes the development of advanced radar-infrared bifunctional materials.

title: Carbon black and hydrogen production from methane pyrolysis: Measured and modeled insights from integrated gas and particle diagnostics in shock tubes
abstract: Methane (CH4) pyrolysis is a promising route to co-produce hydrogen (H2) and carbon black (CB) while avoiding emissions associated with steam-methane reforming and furnace black processes. Model development of pyrolytic CB synthesis requires experimental observations of concurrent gas chemistry, particulate formation, and morphology. This work presents a combined experimental and modeling study of CH4 pyrolysis behind reflected shock waves in 5% CH4/Argon mixtures at post-reflected shock temperatures (T5) of 1850-2450 K and P5 around 4.5 atm. Laser absorption diagnostics quantified CH4, C2H4, and C2H2 mole fractions, while multiwavelength extinction (633 and 1064 nm) resolved time-dependent particle formation and the temperature-dependent evolution of optical maturity. Simulations reproduce small-molecule speciation well, but large variations in predicted polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) persist among models. Coupled gas-particle simulations capture accurate volume fraction (fv) trends and the influence of gas dynamics but underpredict induction times at high T5. Samples collected at the shock tube endwall were analyzed by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to quantify primary particle size distributions and nanostructure arrangement. Image segmentation and manual measurements showed reduced primary particle size growth (dp) with increasing T5, while graphitic nanostructure generally increased. This study provides an integrated benchmark for improving models of CB and H2 production from CH4 pyrolysis by constraining gas-phase kinetics, PAH-driven inception, particle dynamics, and particle maturity. The results highlight that accurate partitioning of mass between particle number and particle size is an important constraint for further model development.

title: Effect of nanoconfinement on hydrogen and deuterium crystal structures
abstract: Nanoconfinement within microporous carbon can profoundly alter the phase behavior of hydrogen (H2), offering a potential route to dense, solid-state H2 storage at moderate pressures. In this study, time-of-flight (ToF) neutron diffraction is used to investigate the crystalline phases of H2 and deuterium (D2) confined within a nanoporous activated carbon (TE7) at low filling fractions (1–50 bar, Θ = 0.33–0.57) and cryogenic temperatures (2.5–13 K). The results reveal the formation of both hexagonal close-packed (HCP) and face-centered cubic (FCC) H2 crystal phases with a higher proportion of FCC phase observed in the micropores. Notably, the FCC phase is stabilized up to 13 K—four times higher temperature than in bulk H2. Double-Voigt line shape analysis of the neutron diffraction data reveals nanoscale crystallite dimensions (≈16 nm FCC, ≈6 nm HCP) suggesting crystallite size restriction in the pores. Additionally, Rietveld refinement shows that greater densification is achieved in smaller pores, in this case sub-nanometer pores. However, only mild unit cell contraction is observed compared with that reported in other studies of H2 confined in nanoporous carbons at low filling fractions. In contrast, D2 exhibits only a broad diffraction feature, indicative of amorphous or nanosized crystallites. These findings provide direct structural evidence demonstrating the effect of nanoconfinement on H2 phase stability, crystal morphology, and density—informing future design of porous materials for solid-state H2 storage.

abstract: : Capillary-driven imbibition is an important oil recovery mechanism in low-permeability reservoirs, particularly during post-fracturing shut-in, but is often hindered by unfavorable wettability, strong oil–solid adhesion, and high oil–water interfacial resistance under high-salinity conditions. Here, ultra-small amphiphilic carboxylate-modified carbon dots (C-CDs) were synthesized through hydrothermal treatment followed by stepwise alkyl and carboxylate functionalization and evaluated as aqueous interfacial modifiers. The C-CDs had an average size of 3.5 ± 0.1 nm, a zeta potential of −40.8 mV, and excellent stability under high salinity and elevated temperature. They reduced oil–water interfacial tension to 2.05 mN/m in 2.0 M NaCl and 1.42 mN/m in 2.0 M CaCl 2 . In crude oil–brine containing divalent ions, the interfacial tension decreased to 1.09 mN/m at 80 °C. Atomic force microscopy showed that C-CDs reduced hydrophobic oil–solid adhesion by more than two orders of magnitude. Quartz crystal microbalance and optical photothermal infrared analyses further demonstrated suppressed crude oil retention, inhibited re-adhesion, and a transition toward an oil-repellent surface state. Core-scale imbibition increased oil recovery from 10.2% with brine to 30.9% with C-CDs, while nuclear magnetic resonance confirmed enhanced oil mobilization from micropores and mesopores. A single exploratory core flooding experiment demonstrated the potential of C-CDs to enhance oil recovery under flow conditions, yielding a final oil recovery of 46.3%. These results reveal an interface-controlled imbibition mechanism involving wettability alteration, weakened oil–solid adhesion, reduced interfacial resistance, and facilitated droplet deformation, highlighting C-CDs as salt-tolerant, thermally stable agents for improving oil recovery in low-permeability, high-salinity porous media.

Phase-based modelling of the morphology of carbon wall depositions in methane pyrolysis reactors
abstract: Methane pyrolysis is an emerging process technology within the hydrogen economy, providing lower carbon emissions than conventional hydrogen production routes. However, this process produces by-product carbon, which can deposit on reactor surfaces. Utilizing carbon deposits formed during methane pyrolysis is necessary to reduce the cost of hydrogen production, but their morphology remains poorly understood. This work hypothesizes that phase changes may explain contrasting carbon depositions. By incorporating hydrogen-to-carbon-ratio-based phase delineation and wall-effect modelling into a two-dimensional laminar reactor simulation, the evolution of carbon morphology is investigated. A discrete sectional model tracks carbon inception and growth, assigning a phase based on hydrogen and carbon content via instantaneous coalescence, and evaluates all nanoparticle collision pairs by size and H/C ratio. The two-dimensional framework enables analysis of diffusion effects relevant to carbon deposition on reactor surfaces, and a three-dimensional post-processor is used to visualize particle morphologies that may occur on the walls. The simulations indicate that phase is a key factor in these depositions: higher temperatures and longer operating times produce larger, more liquid-like spheroids, whereas lower temperatures and shorter operating times yield thin, fractal carbon fibres. The results reveal distinct morphological changes within narrow operating-condition ranges and provide mechanistic insight into how methane pyrolysis conditions influence the structure of carbon wall deposits.

Bottom-up analysis of X-ray diffraction reveals turbostratic melon-like structures in materials commonly assigned to g-C3N4
abstract: Graphitic (sp 2 -hybridized) carbon nitride (g-C 3 N 4 ) is one of the most widely investigated metal-free photocatalysts, yet the atomic structure of materials commonly assigned to g-C 3 N 4 after conventional thermopolymerization remains controversial. The lack of detailed analyses of their X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns has led to multiple and often inconsistent structural interpretations. Moreover, possible stacking configurations, including turbostratic, AB, and ABC sequences, as well as the effects of planar and non-planar layers, have never been investigated systematically. Here, first-principles calculations combined with a bottom-up XRD methodology based on Debye's equation are used to calculate the diffraction fingerprints of the proposed structures and of the main condensation intermediates. This approach discriminates between competing structural models while accounting for crystallite size effects and turbostratic stacking, thereby establishing which structural information can be reliably extracted from XRD patterns. Application of the method to experimental materials synthesized under conventional thermopolymerization conditions demonstrates that the diffraction patterns commonly assigned to g-C 3 N 4 are instead more consistently explained by turbostratic melon-like structures. This interpretation is further supported by elemental analysis and is consistent with previous structural studies based on complementary characterization techniques.

abstract: Laser pyrolysis enables reactive additive manufacturing of porous carbon architectures through highly localized and rapid thermal processing. However, the governing principles of graphitization under non-equilibrium laser conditions remain unclear, particularly the role of transient thermal history and catalytic feedstock chemistry. Here we show that carbon structural evolution is described not by energy density alone, but by an effective thermal dose arising from the coupling of peak temperature and residence time. Using hemoglobin as a model Fe-containing biomolecule, we demonstrate that intrinsic iron is retained during processing and forms Fe-rich catalytic phases during laser-induced graphitization. Despite identical energy densities, varying processing conditions lead to considerably different thermal histories and corresponding degrees of graphitization, revealing the governing role of transient thermal pathways. Thermal modeling combined with experimental analyses identify processing regimes consistent with catalytic activation, where intermediate thermal exposure promotes enhanced graphitic ordering while avoiding excessive thermal degradation. Compared to Fe-free biomolecules, hemoglobin-derived carbons exhibit reduced disorder and increased crystallite size, supporting the role of inherent trace metal centers in conditionally modulating graphitization under non-equilibrium laser processing. These results establish a thermochemical framework for interpreting transient thermal effects on chemical reactions in reactive laser additive manufacturing.

abstract: One-step KOH activation enables the direct conversion of cellulose-based biomass into activated carbon (AC), yet reproducible control over pore structure and carbon yield remains challenging. While many studies emphasize the KOH-to-precursor mass ratio, the water volume used for dissolving a fixed amount of KOH is rarely regarded as an independent parameter. Here, we demonstrate that the amount of water introduced with the KOH solution and its spatial distribution within the cellulose precursor after impregnation, either absorbed into the internal fiber network or retained as excess liquid, govern the thermal transformation pathway and the resulting AC properties. Using paper sheets with a defined absorption capacity as a model precursor, ACs were prepared at constant KOH loading (1:1) while systematically varying the added water volume. This approach establishes distinct initial conditions, ranging from complete solution uptake to excess external solution. Combined thermal analysis (TGA-MS), ATR-FTIR, XRD, XPS, electron microscopy, N 2 adsorption, and SAXS reveal that exceeding the precursor’s absorption capacity promotes early carbonate formation, enhances alkaline degradation, delays char formation, reduces carbon yield from ∼9% for C35 to ∼1% for C20, and strengthens CO 2 -assisted physical activation, leading to larger pores. In contrast, reduced water addition shifts the pathway toward earlier charring, limits the conversion of hydroxide into carbonate, increases yield, and promotes micropore-dominated structures. These findings identify water volume at constant KOH loading as a decisive variable in the investigated solution-impregnation system and demonstrate that it should be controlled alongside the activator-to-precursor mass ratio when targeting reproducible AC properties.

Shock response of carbon fiber microstructure using molecular dynamics simulations
abstract: Carbon fibers are widely used in high-performance structural applications where resistance to extreme dy-namic loading is critical, yet the atomic-scale mechanisms governing their shock response remain poorlyunderstood. In this work, large-scale molecular dynamics simulations are employed to investigate the shock-induced deformation and densification behavior of three-dimensional PAN-derived carbon fiber microstruc-tures constructed from ladder-based precursors. A systematic piston-driven shock framework is appliedto multiple microstructural configurations with varying ladder topologies and orientation, enabling directanalysis of shock propagation, Hugoniot response, and structural evolution. The simulated CF microstruc-tures exhibit the formation of a single steady shock front over piston velocities ranging from 1–6 km/s,with clear evidence of transition away from elasticity. A transition from predominantly elastic behavior toirreversible inelastic shock response is identified at a piston velocity of approximately 3 km/s. Shock ve-locity–particle velocity (Us–Up) relationships display an approximately linear dependence. Atom-istic analysis reveals that shock propagation occurs through distributed network disordering characterizedby fragmentation of six-member carbon rings, increased formation of higher-member rings, and collapseof nanoscale voids. These irreversible topological transformations govern volumetric densification and en-hanced post-shock stiffness. The results demonstrate that shock response in heterogeneous graphitic carbonfiber networks is dominated by progressive microstructural reorganization . This study provides mechanisticinsight into the role of microstructural topology and anisotropy in dynamic densification of carbon fibers,offering an atomistic foundation for interpreting experimental Hugoniot behavior and guiding the design ofimpact-resistant carbon-based materials.

abstract: ABSTRACT Group-IV color centers, such as the silicon-vacancy (SiV) defect, are highly promising for solid-state quantum technologies. However, nanodiamonds typically exhibit significant lattice strain and structural disorder, which degrade their optical properties and hinder the resolution of the fine spectral structure at cryogenic temperatures. High-pressure high-temperature (HPHT) annealing offers a potential route to relax internal strain, although the phase stability of diamond at the nanoscale under such conditions remains poorly constrained. Here, we investigate the structural evolution of nanodiamonds during HPHT annealing using a Paris–Edinburgh press coupled with in situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction at SOLEIL. A dedicated sample assembly combining nanodiamonds – NaCl – Pt enabled accurate pressure–temperature calibration and real-time monitoring of phase transformations. The diffraction data reveal that the onset of diamond-to-graphite transition occurs at approximately 1800 K at 2 GPa and 2120 K at 4 GPa under the applied HPHT heating protocol. These experimentally determined graphitization onsets define a practical pressure–temperature processing window for HPHT annealing of nanodiamonds while avoiding detectable graphitization and provide a calibrated framework for reliable off-beam annealing treatments that avoid graphitization. Photoluminescence measurements on samples annealed below the graphitization threshold show improved optical response, with partial resolution of the SiV fine structure at 12 K. These optical measurements suggest a relationship between nanoscale phase stability and the optical response of individual SiV-containing nanodiamonds following HPHT annealing. The experimentally established HPHT processing window provides a practical framework for the controlled processing of quantum nanodiamonds while avoiding graphitization.

abstract: The design of pitch-based gradient porous carbons is crucial for enhancing capacitive performance, yet the impact of precursor structural evolution on pore formation remains elusive. Herein, a synergistic strategy of small molecule shear and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbonreconfiguration to synthesized submicron/micron rod-like cluster porous carbon with optimal pore size and abundant surface oxygen-containing groups. Experimental and theoretical analysis confirmed that 1.0 nm pores best matched[Zn(H2O)6]2+, maximizing the gradient confinement effect of micropores (0.88 to 1.2 nm) and mesopores (about 3.2 nm) to enable ordered, efficient ion transport and storage. Moreover, the C=O groups provide pseudo-capacitance, which significantly reduced the desolvation energy barrier of [Zn(H2O)6]2+. As a result, the optimized gradient pores carbon exhibited a remarkably specific capacity of 234.6 mAh g-1and 99.4% retention over 65000 cycles. The assembled ZIHCs thus displayed a high energy density of 189.9 Wh kg-1 and a distinguished power density of 65.2 kW kg-1. This work opens the avenue for molecular-level modulation of organic precursors to enable the development of high-performance porous carbon cathodes for ZIHCs.

abstract: Rapid failure of anti-corrosion coatings in complex environments such as wind erosion, sunlight exposure, low temperatures, and high humidity represents a critical bottleneck limiting their long-term protective performance. By constructing a polyurethane (PU) composite with dynamic disulfide bonds and structurally engineered polydopamine-modified Ti3C2Tx (PPM), the PPM/PU composite integrating photothermal, self-healing, early-stage corrosion monitoring, de-icing, and snow melting functions was developed. Under 60 s irradiation with an 808 nm laser at 0.5 W/cm², the surface temperature rose from 28.6 ℃ to 140.3 ℃, achieving rapid repair capability (78.4 %) within 60 s. Furthermore, the ultra-high photothermal conversion effect enables 100 s exposure under sunlight to raise temperatures to 58.5 ℃, achieving rapid repair within 2 min, removing a 3 mm thick ice layer in 2040 s, and demonstrating superior snow melting capabilities. For damaged coating areas, the PPM/PU composite coating could release 1,10-Phenanthroline-5-amine (Phen), provide early-stage warning effects and further delay metal corrosion. Ultimately, a dual-repair strategy under natural sunlight and near-infrared laser illumination was achieved. Moreover, the polyurethane composite exhibited high mechanical strength (2.62 MPa) and toughness (15.36 kJ/m²). This composite design offers a promising pathway for developing multifunctional smart-responsive coatings and multifunctional self-healing materials.

abstract: Developing fibrous microwave absorbers with balanced electromagnetic attenuation, broad effective absorption bandwidth, and radar-scattering suppression capability is important for electromagnetic protection and stealth-related applications. Herein, CoS/C composite nanofibers were fabricated through electrospinning, surface-confined Co-MOF growth, carbonization, and subsequent sulfidation. The obtained one-dimensional composites consist of a PAN-derived conductive carbon framework decorated with CoS nanoparticles, producing CoS/C heterointerfaces and N/O/S-associated defect sites. By regulating the cobalt precursor content, the dielectric response and impedance matching of the composites were effectively tuned. The optimized CSN-6 sample achieves a minimum reflection loss of −61.33 dB at a thickness of 2.27 mm and an effective absorption bandwidth of 6.32 GHz at 2.31 mm, indicating a favorable balance between dielectric attenuation and impedance matching. Electromagnetic-parameter analysis suggests that the enhanced absorption mainly originates from conduction loss in the interconnected carbon-fiber network, CoS/C interfacial polarization, heteroatom/defect-induced dipolar relaxation, and possible multiple reflection/scattering within the fibrous architecture. CST simulations based on the measured electromagnetic parameters further show that the CSN-6-based absorber achieves a maximum simulated radar cross-section reduction of 17.53 dB relative to a perfect electric conductor at 14.56 GHz. Moreover, a simulation-guided gradient periodic unit cell was proposed as a proof-of-concept structural design, generating multiple absorption responses at 2.57, 7.56, and 13.47 GHz. This work provides an interface-regulation and structure-simulation strategy for developing dielectric-loss-dominated CoS/C fibrous microwave absorbers.

title: One-step fabrication of diamond microtubes: A proof of concept
abstract: A one-step methodology for the synthesis of diamond microtubes is proposed. Starting from carbon fibre (CF) substrates, diamond microtube is grown by Microwave Plasma Enhanced Chemical Vapour Deposition (MW PE CVD). Thanks to the graphitic nature of the CF, the substrate decomposition process (etching) takes place at the same time as the diamond layer grows on the CF substrate surface. The balance between the diamond growth rate and the CF etching is the key to obtain self-supporting microtubes. In addition, the nanodiamond seeding pretreatment prior to MW PE CVD growth has been shown to play a main role in the process, adjusting the relationship between diamond growth and carbon etching. This work is a proof of concept of the diamond microtube fabrication, in which the formation process and morphology of the diamond microtubes are structurally evidenced by Scanning Electron Microscopy, while Raman spectroscopy and High-Resolution Transmission Electron Microscopy allow to demonstrate the diamond nature of the microtubes.

title: In-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction investigations of the graphite oxidation by chlorate method
abstract: Chlorate- and permanganate-based oxidations are the two main chemical routes used for the synthesis of graphite oxide (GtO), but the chlorate route has remained unexplored by in-situ methods. The main obstacle has been the need for extremely dangerous fuming nitric acid in the classical Brodie and Staudenmaier graphite oxide synthesis methods. In our earlier study, we developed a chlorate-route method that uses a sulfuric/phosphoric acid mixture instead of nitric acid (Gurzęda method), creating an opportunity for direct in-situ investigation. Here we use in-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction (XRD) to compare graphite oxidation by potassium chlorate in sulfuric/phosphoric acid with standard Hummers oxidation by KMnO 4 in sulfuric acid. Permanganate oxidation results in formation of GO structure with an interlayer distance close to that of stage-1 H 2 SO 4 -graphite intercalation compound. A similar phase is detected also with the Gurzęda method but only as a minor and short-lived intermediate product. It is demonstrated that chlorate oxidation by Gurzęda method follows a distinctly different pathway, yielding “pristine” graphite oxide with substantially larger interlayer spacing due to swelling in aqueous acid/oxidant solution. In-situ characterization also identified important solid reaction product which provides insight into the chlorate oxidation mechanism. Significant difference is observed also during reaction of pristine GtO with water: permanganate-derived GtO delaminates spontaneously, whereas chlorate-derived graphite oxide remains crystalline. These findings provide direct insight into possible nature of the difference in oxidant-dependent properties of GtO and elaborate early stages of graphite oxidation reactions.

title: Surface defect engineering for enhancing tensile properties of carbon fibers
abstract: Polyacrylonitrile (PAN)-based carbon fibers (CFs) suffer from surface flaws including microcracks, irregular roughness, and residual sizing that act as stress concentrators and limit their tensile performance. To address this issue, we introduce an electrochemical etching process that selectively removes surface defects while preserving the internal crystalline structure. The laboratory-fabricated CF (BSCFs) and two commercial CFs (T800 and T1000) were treated in ammonium bicarbonate electrolyte at 0.12 A/m 2 under ambient conditions for 1 to 15 min. AFM, SEM, Raman spectroscopy, XRD, and XPS confirmed the elimination of silicon-based residues originated from PAN precursor fibers and significant reductions in surface roughness of ∼75% for BSCFs, ∼65% for T800, and up to ∼90% for T1000 without changes in interlayer spacing, defect ratio, or density. These improvements translated directly into higher mechanical performance. T1000 showed strength increases of ∼24% (from 6.3 ± 0.6 to 7.8 ± 0.6 GPa) and modulus increases of ∼21% (from 294.1 ± 20.1 to 355.7 ± 23.8 GPa), respectively. Finite element simulations further reveal that surface roughness induces stress concentration, leading to premature failure, whereas electrochemical etching effectively alleviates these stress concentrations, thereby enhancing the tensile performance. These values are comparable to the world best performance CF such as T1200 (tensile strength of 8 GPa and modulus of 315 GPa). In addition, the interfacial shear strength increased to 43.3 ± 2.9 MPa for T1000, corresponding to improvements 4.4% relative to unetched fibers. Overall, this work demonstrates electrochemical etching as a practical, scalable, energy-efficient approach to high-performance CFs.

Wafer-scale single-crystalline graphene transferred from SiC exhibiting Landau quantization
abstract: Producing large-area single-crystalline graphene is key to realizing its full potential in advanced applications, including twistronics. Yet, controlling graphene growth kinetics to avoid grain boundaries or multilayer growth remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate the possibility to obtain single-crystalline graphene free of multilayer domains via a facile one-step delamination of epitaxial graphene from silicon carbide (SiC). We find that this is enabled by a specific surface reconstruction of 4H-SiC(0001) that we achieve under our growth conditions. The high crystalline quality of graphene after delamination and transfer from the SiC substrate is confirmed by the observation of key fingerprints of Dirac fermions in quantum transport: ambipolar charge transport, Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations up to filling factor ν = 4 N + 2 = 74 , with N the Landau index, Berry phase of π , and half-integer quantum Hall effect in cm-sized crystals. The scalability of our process, explored with recycled 4”-SiC wafers, represents an advance toward large-scale integration of high-performance graphene applications.

Defect engineering in graphene via ion irradiation: A universal scaling framework
abstract: Defect engineering is an effective strategy for tailoring graphene’s physical and chemical properties for applications in nanoelectronics, sensing, catalysis, energy storage, and membrane technologies. Here, we employ quantitative defect analysis and molecular dynamics simulations to understand the concentration and structure of defects produced by energetic ion-irradiation. Exfoliated graphene layers are irradiated with 30 keV H, Li, C, Si and Ge ions to various fluences and the resulting defect density and type determined by Raman spectroscopy. Molecular dynamics simulations are shown to reproduce the observed ion-mass dependence of defect production for heavier ions but to underestimate the relative defect production rate for H irradiation. In contrast, an analytical displacement cross-section based on a fixed displacement energy (i.e. 22 eV) accurately scales the data for all ions, thereby providing a basis for universal scaling. Finally, we show that the nature of the residual defects evolves with increasing defect density, and that this behavior is independent of the irradiating ion species. This combined experimental and theoretical approach provides a comprehensive picture of ion–graphene interactions and establishes universal scaling rules for defect engineering in two-dimensional materials.

Curvature mapping of overlapping pores in disordered carbons using scanning electron nanobeam diffraction
abstract: The bending and orientation of layers, along with any potential pore structures in disordered carbons, are crucial for their performance in many applications. Therefore, it is essential to characterize them. Traditionally, detection and analysis of fringes in high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM) images are used for characterization. However, fringes are affected by instrumental artifacts, such as spectral modulation by the microscope's contrast transfer function and multiple overlapping structures in projection, which can lead to misinterpretation. Here, we propose to visualize and further analyze the nature of curved, graphite-like stacked layers in disordered carbons by examining changes in Bragg disc orientation in scanning electron nanobeam diffraction (SEND) patterns. The new approach uses non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) to reduce the complexity of the SEND patterns. It enables the detection and characterization of curved layers over a larger field of view than is readily achievable with individual HR-TEM images, thereby enhancing the statistical relevance of the methodology. Moreover, the approach yields structural information about curved layers of multiple intertwined and overlapping regions. It allows separation of contributions to overlapping layers of different pores and enables independent analysis of their curvatures. The potential of the new approach is demonstrated by analyzing simulated and experimentally measured SEND data from disordered carbons.

Metal-Controlled Excited-State Dynamics in Carbon Dots: Linking Singlet Oxygen Generation and Visible-Light Antiviral Activity
abstract: Understanding how precursor chemistry and processing control the photophysical and photochemical properties of carbon dots (C-dots) is essential for their rational design as visible-light-responsive nanomaterials. We investigated C-dots obtained by thermal decomposition of ethylenediaminetetraacetate (EDTA)-based precursors, Na 2 H 2 EDTA, Na 2 [Mn(EDTA)], and Na 2 [Zn(EDTA)], to study how metal–EDTA chemistry affects carbonization, excited-state dynamics, singlet oxygen generation, and antiviral activity. Structural characterization shows that all samples are predominantly amorphous, but Mn remains highly dispersed within a disordered carbon matrix, whereas Zn partially segregates into nanocrystalline ZnO domains. Time-resolved photoluminescence and femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy reveal that metal incorporation modifies the balance between radiative and nonradiative relaxation pathways. Zn C-dots show the strongest and most persistent ground-state bleach, indicating a larger population of long-lived trapped excited states. Under 450 nm irradiation, singlet oxygen is the dominant detectable reactive oxygen species. Despite the faster indocyanine green (ICG) bleaching of Zn C-dots, Mn C-dots exhibit the highest ICG-based apparent singlet-oxygen quantum yield (Φ Δ = 0.193), followed by Zn C-dots (0.080) and undoped C-dots (0.019). Antiviral activity follows the same order, with Mn C-dots achieving 99.98% vaccinia virus inactivation. These results show that singlet oxygen generation is governed not simply by light harvesting or excited-state population, but by the efficiency with which long-lived excited states sensitize molecular oxygen.

Signatures of a high-temperature collective electronic phase with superconductivity-like characteristics and a giant pressure effect in networks of boron-doped ultrathin carbon nanotubes
abstract: ABSTRACT We present data consistent with a high-temperature collective electronic phase with superconductivity-like characteristics in three dimensional networks of boron doped, ultrathin carbon nanotubes (CNTs) grown inside the ∼5 Å channels of ZSM 5 zeolite. Confinement stabilizes (2,1) CNTs that are otherwise dynamically unstable, while boron doping shifts the Fermi level toward a van Hove singularity, as supported by ab-initio calculations. The resulting CNT network exhibits multiple, mutually consistent signatures of an electronic condensate with the typical characteristics of a high temperature superconductor at ambient pressure. DC magnetization and AC susceptibility measurements reveal the onset of a Meissner response between 220 and 250 K, with compacted samples achieving up to 93% of full diamagnetic screening. Electrical transport shows a sharp resistive transition with extrapolated T c ≈ 239 K and vanishing resistance in optimized samples. Specific heat measurements display a reproducible anomaly at 233–236 K that broadens under magnetic field, consistent with strong fluctuations. Point contact spectroscopy identifies three energy gaps, including a leading gap of ∼30 meV whose temperature dependence follows BCS expectations for T c ≈ 224 K, and exhibits particle–hole symmetry and Andreev reflection. Remarkably, applying pressures below 0.1 kbar enhances T c by nearly 100 K and modulates the room temperature resistance by more than three orders of magnitude, suggesting a pressure driven 1D to 3D crossover in the CNT network. These results identify boron doped ultrathin CNT networks as a promising carbon-based platform for near ambient temperature superconductivity and reveal an unusually large pressure sensitivity with potential technological relevance.

Relating Pore-Network Descriptors to TFSI- Dynamics and Electrochemical Charging in Templated Carbon Electrodes
abstract: How network-sensitive mesopore sorption descriptors relate to TFSI - displacement and cell-level charging remains poorly understood for hierarchical porous carbons. Herein, we compare hard-templated CMK-3 and combined hard-and-salt-templated ST-CMK-3 electrodes using network-aware sorption, quantitative TEM, 19 F PFG NMR, and electrochemistry. The CMK-3 sorption response is adequately described by the chain-limit model, whereas ST-CMK-3 is better represented by a model permitting higher effective coordination, indicating departure from a simple chain-like mesopore response. Analysis of selected TEM micrographs reveals comparable local fringe spacing and retained mesoscale periodic contrast, but lower ROI-scale FFT annular anisotropy and shorter image texture correlation scales for ST-CMK-3, indicating weaker directional concentration within the selected spatial-frequency band despite comparable local coherency. Two-component analysis of the 19 F PFG NMR attenuation yields a larger constraint-dependent point estimate of the effective transverse TFSI - diffusion coefficient for ST-CMK-3 in physically constrained fits at matched bulk-like ex-pore signal fractions. Although fitted parameters reach bounds and the nominal conditional transverse 95% confidence intervals overlap, this ordering persists across the tested ex-pore fractions. It also matches the ordering of effective transverse coefficients previously derived from 19 F 2D EXSY NMR exchange rates within an exchange model, although the methods probe different observables. In 1 M aqueous LiTFSI, ST-CMK-3 delivers higher low-rate capacitance and energy density at comparable average power, but lower high current capacitance retention and slower capacitive relaxation. These pair-specific observations are consistent with complementary contributions from mesopore-associated electrolyte access and redistribution and micropore-associated charge storage and equilibration, without isolating connectivity as the causal variable.
